extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and scientists studying logic, induction, and the scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for forming, testing, and expressing inductive and deductive reasoning (use of syllogisms, general propositions, and trains of reasoning) in philosophical and scientific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the general theorem in its broadest form
rubrics_metrics.description: When an induction from observation or experiment justifies a conclusion about one case, it justifies an indefinite multitude; ascertain and declare the theorem in its broadest form of generality so as to place before the mind the whole of what the evidence must prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulating the general proposition broadly exposes the full extent of what the evidence must support and helps ensure we weigh sufficiency of the experience appealed to. Example: rather than stating a single-case conclusion, express the encompassing general rule that would have to hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generalization to detect insufficiency by reductio
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting an inference into a universal generality increases the chance of detecting insufficient premises, because a false generalization will often include counterinstances already known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proposed generalization would imply a fact known or suspected to be false, that reveals insufficiency of the original observations. Use reductio ad impossibile on the general form to expose defects in evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent doubtful reasoning in syllogistic form
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is any doubt about the validity of reasoning, throw it into the form of an induction followed by a deduction (syllogism) to test its conclusiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syllogistic form is not necessarily how we actually think, but it furnishes a mode in which reasoning may always be represented and which is 'admirably calculated' to bring inconclusiveness to light. Use syllogisms to make implicit premises explicit and test them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate investigation into induction then application (two-step process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide inquiry into (1) establishing general formulæ (induction) that determine what inferences may be drawn, and (2) applying those formulæ to particular cases (deduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make inductions once and record them as general propositions for later syllogistic application; this aids memory and orderly application of past experience to new cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use general propositions as convenient, not essential, tools
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions are conveniences for reasoning and memory, not necessary preconditions of correct inference; they facilitate testing and repeatable application of past inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that very sagacious minds can reason without explicit generalities, but for general scientific assurance it is advisable to adopt and record general formulæ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of consecrated but insufficient maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations formed on insufficient evidence may harden into maxims and habitually mislead once particulars are forgotten; such maxims should be subject to revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the convenience of general language with vigilance: revise general propositions when new evidence shows they were grounded on insufficient instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major premise should express sufficiency of evidence (avoid petitio principii)
rubrics_metrics.description: The major of a syllogism should be an affirmation that the evidence is sufficient to authorize the conclusion (i.e., the result of a proper induction), not a disguised restatement of the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid begging the question by ensuring the major is supported by independent induction. The major is an assertion about the sufficiency of evidence, not merely a restatement of what is to be proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the psychological test of sufficiency from induction itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that evidence is sufficient is a retrospective testing operation, not part of the original inductive act; testing that the process was correctly performed is distinct from the inference itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the mental act of reviewing whether an induction was done rightly with the inductive inference; make explicit testing procedures when scientific certainty is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify the minor premise (establish resemblance/marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The minor premise affirms resemblance between the new case and known cases in certain attributes and must be investigated—sometimes by further argument or induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor premises are often not obvious and may need proof (e.g., by observation, testimony, or other inductions). Scrutinize and establish the resemblance asserted in the minor before accepting the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow nested or chained inductions (trains of reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex conclusions often require a train of reasoning—multiple syllogisms/inductions chained so that one induction brings the case within the scope of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and unpack multi-step chains (e.g., A is observed -> infer B; B then permits inference C; etc.). When reasoning involves inferred marks-of-marks, trace and assess each inductive link's evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and determine distinguishing marks for legitimate induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide once for all what marks distinguish cases to which an induction may be legitimately extended; these marks are the criteria used later to identify new cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly register the criteria (marks) by which a class is defined for the induction. Later identification of a new case involves checking for those marks, possibly by other marks established through further inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal logic to test consistency, not as substitute for empirical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal logic (conversion, opposition, syllogism) is primarily the logic of consistency—useful to ensure inferences accord with general formulæ—but it does not itself establish empirical truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply formal logical rules to check that conclusions follow consistently from stated general propositions; still ground general propositions in observed instances to secure truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: When practical certainty is required, make the testing operation explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Although ordinary reasoning may omit the formal test, in scientific inquiry insist that reasoning pass through the general-proposition test to ensure the sufficiency of evidence is examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert tentative direct inferences into induction+deduction forms to verify them. The extra formal step is a security for correctness and should be applied when error would be consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that the real premises are individual observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when general propositions are used, the ultimate grounds of inference are the original particular observations which justify the induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind the observational basis underlying majors: be prepared to revisit the particulars if a general proposition appears suspect; do not treat general forms as independent of their empirical roots.
